# The Structure of Othering: How Language Shapes Division

There exists a particular kind of text that reveals something profound about human communication precisely because it withholds specific content. Imagine a passage composed entirely of incomplete sentence fragments, each containing blanks left unfilled. Rather than making concrete accusations or offering detailed observations, such a text presents only the scaffolding of judgment—structure without specific content. In doing so, it exposes the underlying architecture of how we speak about others.

What becomes immediately apparent in this kind of writing is its persistent grammatical pattern. Nearly every fragment begins by referencing "they," establishing an unrelenting us-versus-them framing that saturates the entire passage. This repeated invocation of an unnamed collective does more than organize the sentences; it constructs an invisible boundary between the speaker's group and the others being discussed. The reader never learns who "they" are, yet the constant repetition ensures that a division is felt on every line.

The emotional tenor of these fragments is equally telling. Many of the phrases express judgment, criticism, or open disapproval directed at the unnamed group. They gesture toward failings, shortcomings, and objectionable behaviors without ever specifying what these might be. The blanks remain empty, but the disapproving posture is unmistakable—a reminder that condemnation can be communicated through tone and structure alone, independent of any particular charge.

Yet the passage is not entirely one-sided. Several fragments attempt to acknowledge context or extend a measure of empathy. They note the limited perspectives available to the group, or gesture toward the difficult circumstances that might explain their situation. These moments of apparent understanding complicate the picture, suggesting an effort at fairness or compassion. Still, even these empathetic gestures remain trapped within the same "they"-centered framework, ultimately reinforcing rather than dissolving the separation between groups.

Taken as a whole, the overall effect is illuminating. The text demonstrates how language itself can perpetuate othering and generalization, regardless of what specific accusations might eventually fill the blanks. Whether the unnamed group is praised, criticized, or pitied, the very grammar of "us" and "them" performs a kind of division on its own. In this way, the passage serves as a quiet warning: the words we choose, and the structures we habitually reach for, may shape our relationships with others long before any particular content is supplied.

# The Grammar of "They"

There is a peculiar architecture to prejudice, and it can be found not in the content of any single accusation but in the structure that makes all accusations possible. This piece takes that structure as its subject. Rather than argue against any particular bigotry, it assembles a series of open-ended sentence fragments—each one beginning to say something about an unnamed "they"—and lets the pattern speak for itself.

"They always..." "They never..." "They think they can..." "They don't understand that..." "You can't trust them because..." Each fragment opens onto a familiar rhetorical shape, a groove worn smooth by repetition. The sentences remain deliberately incomplete, their objects unnamed, their grievances unspecified. This is the point. By withholding the identity of "they," the work strips away the particular so that the general machinery of othering becomes visible. We are left looking not at what is said about any group, but at the very grammar through which one group defines itself against another.

What emerges is a recognition that the language of division is portable. The same constructions serve to condemn the foreigner, the neighbor, the rival faction, the unfamiliar faith, the opposing party. Fill in the blank with whatever population you fear or resent, and the sentence functions identically. The "they" is a variable, endlessly substitutable, while the grammar surrounding it remains fixed. In this way the work demonstrates that prejudice is less a set of beliefs about specific people than a habit of speech—a reflexive way of organizing the world into those who belong and those who do not.

There is something unsettling in this demonstration, and it is meant to be. Because the fragments are incomplete, readers are invited—almost compelled—to finish them. And in the moment of completion, we supply our own "they," our own assumptions, our own quietly held resentments. The blank becomes a mirror. Whatever we pour into it reveals the divisions we already carry, the categories we have inherited or constructed, the ease with which we, too, slip into the vocabulary of us-versus-them.

By refusing resolution, the piece resists becoming a lecture about any specific injustice. It does not tell readers whom to defend or whom to blame. Instead it asks a more difficult and more intimate question: What do you assume when you hear the word "they"? In exposing the shared syntax beneath countless particular hatreds, the work suggests that the first step toward dismantling prejudice is not to correct our conclusions but to notice the sentence we were already building—and to hesitate before we finish it.
outputs.L5:
# Once, They Learned to Trust

Once, there lived a small group of travelers who never spoke to strangers. They kept to themselves, wary of every unfamiliar face they passed along the road. Their journey was long, and their hearts were heavy with suspicion.

Sometimes, when the nights grew cold and the fire burned low, they wished they had someone to share their stories with. But fear held them back. What if the strangers meant harm? What if trust led to betrayal?

One evening, a weary traveler approached their camp. He asked only for a place to rest. At first, they hesitated. They exchanged uncertain glances, unsure whether to welcome him or send him away.

Sometimes, the smallest act of kindness changes everything. They decided to let him stay. That night, the stranger shared tales of distant lands, of mountains touched by clouds and rivers that sparkled like glass. They listened, spellbound, and something inside them softened.

By morning, they realized how much they had missed simple human connection. The walls they had built around themselves began to crumble.

Once, they had feared the world. Now, they understood that sometimes the greatest treasures come from opening your heart to others. And they never traveled alone again.
